Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties in elastography is severely impaired by motion artifacts caused by patients breathing or muscle movements during scans that utilize surface elastography methods. Developing elastography systems with the ability to estimate tissue mechanical properties at specific depths could help mitigate this issue. Researchers have explored various strategies for depth-restricted elastography estimation, primarily focusing on the challenges of gathering reference data to determine material parameters. In contrast, our novel virtual origin synthetic aperture approach targets the precision of lateral displacement estimation in ultrasound elastography. By constructing a synthetic aperture at a designated reference depth, the approach generates precise lateral displacement estimates at that depth, without requiring a actual virtual origin. Our simulations and experiments using a gelatin phantom and a human subject demonstrated the accuracy of this method, with results showing a 2.5 mm precision in estimating the distance between two gelatin phantom samples and a 4 mm precision in estimating the depth of a human subject's fat layer.

We introduce a new representation called the Rational Pseudocode (RPS) to compare and link automatic reasoning algorithms with manually constructed proof demonstrations. RPS structures comprise of formulas and function symbols similar to those used in proof languages, yet they also incorporate the semantics of first-order logic. We show that numerous well-known algorithms, including resolution, refinement-based methods, and tableau systems, can be effectively represented as RPS programs. Furthermore, we develop a query-based approach to establish an alignment between an RPS program and a proof tree, which in turn enables the linking of an algorithm to a specific demonstration. This connection preserves the original meaning of both the algorithm and the proof, ensuring that the assigned label accuracies are meaningful and valid. We demonstrate this approach on a subset of the recent CLOTTO challenge data, showcasing our method's capability to accurately compare algorithms with human-constructed proofs.

In the context of high-dimensional data with a large number $n$ of points, we develop an efficient clustering algorithm called \textsc{Dymekmeans-$k$} that leverages a key technique called \emph{sorting with comparisons}, thereby obtaining nearly optimal results for a wide range of data dimensions $d$. Specifically, \textsc{Dymekmeans-$k$} yields a data structure known as a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate \emph{center tree}, which serves as a compact, tree-like representation of the input data's clustering structure, in time $O(nd\cdot f_{\text{sort}}(n)+n\cdot \text{asc}(n)\cdot k\cdot \text{poly}(d))$ for data with a natural ordering, where $f_{\text{sort}}(n)$ captures the time required to perform a sorting operation for data of size $n$, and $\text{asc}(n)$ represents the time to determine the order relationship between pairs of data points, thereby yielding a significant improvement over prior approaches for data with a high dimensionalities, such as those found in certain applications of genetic data, certain types of image or signal processing, and certain aspects of web-based data analysis.

In large-scale autonomous systems like swarms and self-driving networks, cooperation and trust are critical for achieving shared goals under uncertainty. To explore the fundamental requirements for effective cooperation, we developed a hierarchical model of pursuit-evasion games with multiple agents, where some act as pursuers seeking to discover and capture targets, while others evade them. We studied how the success of target agents is influenced by the ratio of pursuers to targets, the complexity of their surrounding environment, and the randomness of target movements. Through extensive simulations, our research uncovered several key findings regarding the essential conditions for cooperation in this context, including the necessity for a significant disparity between the number of pursuers and targets, as well as sufficient spatial freedom to facilitate successful captures.

At the TeV scale, collisions between high-energy muon and ion ($\mu N$) or high-energy muon and muon ($\mu \mu$) can resemble substructure similar to that found in hadron collisions, yet with distinct characteristics resulting from the directed nature of the incoming muon beams. This study focuses on developing an effective method for estimating vector boson production in these $\mu N$ and $\mu \mu$ collisions by accounting for the leading jet and substructure variables, and provides findings relevant to beyond Standard Model searches for vector boson pairs within leptonic decay channels.

In complex environments with multiple interconnected components, developing effective learning systems for multiple related tasks is crucial. We examine a case where a reinforcement learning agent must manage multiple tasks linked in a modular way, with some tasks affecting others via inter-domain interactions. Our study focuses on an agent that employs a model-based approach to learn the dynamics of each task in isolation, despite their interconnections. A key challenge in this scenario arises from destructive interference between tasks, where the agent must reconcile conflicting goals triggered by the same event. To tackle this issue, we show that using separate modules for each task and incorporating an internal incentive to cooperate among them is crucial. By constructing a unified policy from the outputs of individual modules, the agent can mitigate the adverse effects of interference and even leverage it to gain a benefit. Our results illustrate the benefits of modular design and model-based methods in this context, where both result in significant performance gains over non-model-based and non-modular approaches.

This paper officially marks the 80th anniversary of Gödel's Completeness Theorem, whose proof by Gödel unexpectedly led to the discovery of a pertinent Incompleteness phenomenon.  To honor this significant event, we are gathering renowned logicians, mathematicians, and computer scientists at Lake Como to discuss cutting-edge research and theoretical applications of mathematical logic.  The conference schedule spans from April 24th to the 28th, 2007, with the proceedings to be published in a subsequent volume of these conference proceedings.
This study extends Guysen's three spheres theorem from harmonic functions to eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator in Clifford analysis.

InInverse Issues represent prior statements or information that subsequent prior statements contradict. Identifying such prior statements that are contradicted by prior information is known as posterior extraction. This task is crucial in managing and evaluating prior information. We have formulated an inverse issue network (IIN) to address posterior extraction. This IIN consists of a generator that takes prior information as input and produces issues, then a discriminator that verifies the generated issues' validity based on prior information. Both components can be trained using adversarial training. To enhance performance, we introduced a regularization term that encourages prior information to which the generated issues are added to be inconsistent with subsequent prior information. This regularization term was incorporated into the discriminator's training objective. We evaluated the IIN on multiple datasets and found it to outperform the baseline model across various evaluation metrics.

We provide an innovative approach to examining the existence of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems governed by fractional differential equations. By reinterpreting existing breakthroughs, we demonstrate that nonlinear differential equations with non-integer orders cannot support invariant surfaces subjected to specific stability constraints. Consequently, this proof of a previously reported result in [12] expands on the original proof from [21].

The interstellar medium is capable of scrutinizing the path that an electron takes as it passes through it, leaving behind a telltale pattern as it interacts with a pulsar's emitted radiation. This phenomenon, known as scintillation, allows astronomers to study the electron density within the Milky Way galaxy. A team of researchers has conducted an extensive analysis of the pulsar B1133+16's radiation over a decade, observing the persistence of a pattern of scintillation that indicates a association with a particular structure in the galaxy. By combining their findings with data from other sources, the researchers believe this pattern may be linked to a gas cloud that is moving towards the galaxy's center, and as such, may provide valuable insights into the galaxy's composition and evolution.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the model incorporates a pitch-independent and pitch-dependent stream of dilated convolutions to enhance efficiency while maintaining pitch sensitivity. Secondly, a new learning objective is introduced to leverage the correlation between input frequencies and waveform period. Experimental evaluations under both unconditional and conditional generation settings demonstrate the improved pitch control and quality of QPNet in comparison to WN and other baseline models. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/pan-xy/qpnet.
The bicategory of shadows, previously established in a companion paper, is shown to be equivalent to the bicategory of tracks under a specific rebranding.

Our research focuses on developing a head-free, audio-based method to localize speech in a noisy environment with background talkers, a challenging scenario often encountered in real-life situations. Unlike many previous studies that used artificial sound sources or focused on localized tones, our approach addresses a key issue: when multiple speakers occupy the same frequency band, signal processing techniques struggle to separate and pinpoint the source of each individual voice. Our solution involves a two-part strategy. First, we use a novel application of independent component analysis to assign an unambiguous location to each auditory pole, even in presence of significant overlap and frequency sharing. Second, we employ a Bayesian approach to associate the computed sound sources with speaking humans in the surrounding environment. Our results show that both approaches can handle complex scenarios with up to 16 frequency bands and 6 talking humans in different locations. Our data-driven method yields accurate predictions about the visual counterparts of auditory sources, with our code available online for further modification and use.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been propelled by the potential GNNs have to handle dynamic, complex data such as citations and protein interactions. Several critical GNN applications including ranking, classification, and regression can be affected by the distance between nodes, thus it is essential to incorporate distance information into these models. Most current GNN techniques are based on Euclidean geometry, but they are not well-suited for the majority of real-world datasets that operate under a different geometric framework. This tendency needs a critical re-evaluation as most real-world datasets, including those mentioned above, use a Lorentzian geometry that determines their properties and behaviors. To address this issue, we are introducing a novel GNN called LGL, which is capable of handling Lorentzian graph structures and can incorporate distance information that is essential for many real-world datasets. Experimental evaluations of the LGL model on multiple datasets consistently show its superior performance compared to existing GNN approaches.

This research focuses on a problem where we identify unknown components of a structure within a enclosed space that contains moving air. Unlike traditional problems, where we calculate the structure's and air's responses to given inputs, we now aim to determine the input that will result in a specified response from the structure and the air within the space. This problem is highly complex and can be mathematically represented as a nonlinear inverse problem. To solve for the input, we use a novel gradient-based algorithm that requires the solution of several nonlinear forward problems and their derivatives. Initially, we tested and validated our method on a sample problem with both analytical and numerical solutions. Next, we applied our algorithm to a more complex problem with a rigid wall, determining the force required to result in a specific vibration pattern from the structure and the air within the space.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model based on the Tsallis entropy concept, and explore the framework's implications. This framework, which incorporates a temperature parameter, offers a potential link to neuroscience explanations. We show that the Tsallis-like model can simulate biased decision-making behaviors under both fair and unfair probability conditions, and that its hyperparameter effects on impulsive behavior can be understood through the temperature parameter's influence on cognitive processes. Furthermore, we find that the model's temperature parameter can be related to neuroscience variables such as dopamine levels, and that it provides a plausible account of performance on the Iowa Gambling Task.

We outline the fundamental principles of harmonic gauge theories in a linearized gravitational framework, focusing on the implications of the harmonic gauge condition in both its strict and relaxed forms. We then examine the behavior of a massless spin-two field within a background metric that varies smoothly, before delving into the details of harmonic gauge theories in the context of a symmetric tensor field. We also consider the specific case of a flat background, utilizing a perturbative approach to expand the harmonic gauge condition to its second-order terms in the gravitational field strength.

For a quadratic Hamiltonian, we transform Weyl-Wigner's classical and Moyal's quantum fluctuation dissipation theorems into Weyl-Wigner representations, utilizing phase space approaches. This transformation enables us to reinterpret the Poisson bracket averages as Gaussian moments in classical phase space and Gaussian expectations in quantum phase space. As a result, we obtain Weyl-Wigner representations of the classical and quantum canonical equilibrium conditions, which can be expressed in a unified theorems' framework. This unified framework consists of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the response function theorem, and the Onsager reciprocity relations theorem. It is necessary to note that the Weyl-Wigner form of these theorems differs significantly from their original form.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been intellectually intriguing scientists for nearly eight decades. Since its theoretical introduction in 1934 by G.T. Kennedy, this concept has found applications across various fields including quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, and electronics. We reflect on the historical development of negative absolute temperature, its theoretical framework, as well as its computational and experimental realization. Additionally, we explore its emerging uses in quantum dot electronics, cavity quantum electrodynamics, and solid-state mesoscopic systems. Our optimistic outlook suggests the future of negative absolute temperature is marked by continued advancement in related technologies and expansive areas of its implementation.

Within the most fundamental scoto-seesaw framework, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, dark matter behavior, and the stability of the vacuum state. This analysis involves modifying the $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ invariant scalar sector to include three complex singlet scalar fields to mediate the neutrino mass generation and dark matter interaction. By establishing relationships between the neutrino mass and dark matter particle behavior, we determine the parameters that influence the effective dark matter interaction strength and neutrino oscillation probabilities. Additionally, we identify the conditions for vacuums to be stable and viable dark matter particle properties.

Orbital mixing, resulting from cubic crystal field symmetry being broken, leads to significant rearrangement of spectral weight, particularly in transition metal compounds with partially filled $e_g$ states. The extent of this shift, however, greatly depends on the degree of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital mixing. We determine this degree of mixing using the <110> direction's $d$-projected density of states and $e_g$-$t_{2g}$ splitting in Nudist formalism. We address the issue of comparing the structure of relative quantum topological invariants in the context of birational geometric changes. Given two projective varieties, $X$ and $Y$, that are algebraically linked through a morphism of the type $\text{Proj}(S) \to \text{Proj}(T)$, generating their coordinate rings, we show how to extend the birational connection to the level of Kauffman-skein quasi-operators. These operators act on the space of linear combinations of colored and framed links in the ambient space, and we establish isomorphism between the reduced parts of the operator algebras on $X$ and $Y$. Our approach involves incorporating the principles of quantum invariant properties and applying Morita Morita-equivalence induced alterations to the operator algebras, which in turn are generated by the Morita Morita-invariants of the Kauffman-skein operators associated with the Seiberg-Witten 4-manifolds defined by $X$ and $Y$.

The concerns about artificially generated medical images being misleading to poorly trained machine learning models are legitimate, which can lead to severe consequences if they are used in critical applications, such as diagnosing patients with COVID-19 from X-rays. In response to these worries, researchers are starting to explore techniques for detecting and rectifying manipulated images, known as fact-checking in the context of medical imaging. In our study, we developed an innovative approach to flag and address artificially created X-rays that contain fabricated lung lesion information and, in turn, altered COVID-19 diagnosis confidence in a deep learning model. Our results show that this approach can accurately pinpoint both the image and the modification associated with it and boost the model's confidence in correct COVID-19 diagnoses accurately, without overcorrecting healthy images. In particular, our approach successfully recovered authentic image information and restored the confidence of the model to its original state for healthy images not affected by COVID-19. In addition, our approach proved capable of rectifying both single and combined image modifications and even those created with different modulation depths. In order to facilitate reproducibility and ease the burden on limited clinical resources, we shared the code and data associated with this research project publicly.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and analysis. It is capable of handling vectors of any length and can perform calculations on high-density sets of variables. The program can automatically select the most significant features of a dataset and produce results in selected features, making it easier to understand complex data. ViDaExpert also incorporates metrics and algorithms from the field of topological data analysis. The program generates reports in PDF format detailing its findings.
